18:The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
19:On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says of every file the application creates: the container runs as the user rather than as root inside the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions, never owned by Administrators or another account.
21:#### Missing Podman
23:Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:
25:- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
26:- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
27:- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux
29:A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.
31:#### Podman Machine
33:On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.
35:#### Podman Access
37:Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.
39:#### Image
41:Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
42:Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run `piton build` to check its work.
43:A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what its runs in a container need, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
44:While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.
46:#### Mounts
48:What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in the container, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, on every platform, each location given at its place relative to the project directory under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, and the run works in `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`. So a harness that keys its sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations, follows.
50:##### Spec
52:A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the Suspense fluency file, read only; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.
54:##### Question
56:A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container, and the Suspense fluency file, read only. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.
58:Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
59:Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both the code location and the spec location.
60:A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.
62:#### Paths
64:On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as `/workspace-old`. A path that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and opens nothing.
66:#### Volumes
68:The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing one costs only a login.
69:The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.
70:Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
72:##### Context
74:the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
76:can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried over; each conversation starts fresh.
78:#### Logging In
80:When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
81:The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.
83:#### Guards
85:A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.
87:#### Spec Build
89:A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference, and that build succeeds whenever the spec is sound: it owns the reference files it finds, through the manifest in the mounted `.piton` directory, and places the shape's guidance in the scratch directory standing in for the code location, where it goes nowhere. A build there that fails fails only because of the spec, never because of what the container leaves out, so its errors are the run's own to fix. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.

content.content:
image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The
        build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as
        `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built
        against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which
        command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't
        run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run
        `piton build` to check its work.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what
        its runs in a container need, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in
    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

content.text:
I couldn't see the actual error, so I made the spec cover the likeliest causes of a first-login image failure. If you paste the error text, I can narrow it down to one. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

**Likeliest causes:**
- **Host binaries copied into the image.** If the build copies the host's harness or piton binary in, it can't run on macOS or Windows, because the image is Linux.
- **A brand-new harness volume owned by root.** The container runs as you, so the login command can't write its credentials.
- **Two image builds at once.** The login and the Welcome or Settings check can each start a build of the same image, and they collide.

## What changed in the spec

**Image** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#image`)
- **Linux tools only:** the image is always Linux. Each harness and piton is installed from its own Linux release at the version found on the host, never copied from the host. Anything not found or not published for Linux is installed at its latest.
- **Isolated build:** the build gets a fresh temporary directory containing only the Containerfile the app writes. It never sees the project or your home folder, and needs only the network.
- **One build at a time:** a run, login or check that needs an image already being built waits for that build instead of starting another.
- **No half-built images:** the image is tagged only after the build succeeds, so a failed or interrupted build is never mistaken for a good one.
- **Full errors:** a failed build shows the step it failed at and everything Podman printed, and the same goes to a build log kept beside the preferences.

**Logging in** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#logging-in`)
- **Image first:** the login view builds the image if it's missing or out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and the build output. The login command starts only after the build succeeds.
- **Retry:** if the build fails, the login view shows why, with a "Try again" button.
- **Volume ready before first use:** the harness's volume is created with `podman volume create` before the first login. It is mounted so the container's user owns it and can write to it, for example with Podman's `:U` option.
- **HOME:** the container's home folder, where the volume is mounted beneath it as `~/.claude`, is owned by that same user, so the first login can write its credentials.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791140688-PodmanImageCreationError.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`:
  - `#image`: the Containerfile, build context, build lock, tagging only on success, and error output.
  - `#logging-in`: build before login, Try again, volume creation and ownership, HOME.
  - `#volumes`: where each volume is mounted.
  - `#podman-access`: for failures where Podman can't be reached.
- `WelcomeScope` and `SettingsWindowScope`: their login checks and buttons, which share the one build.
